“Father kept on his desk,” Martin Freud relates, “a kind of unbound diary in the form of large sheets of white paper upon which he recorded in a most laconic way those events of each day that seemed to him important.” At the top of the first of the sheets on which he made his recordings in his usual Gothic script, Freud wrote: Kürtzeste Chronik (Shortest Chronicle). Why shortest? Perhaps because the recordings were begun in 1929, when he was seventy-three and felt he had not much longer to live.

His previous writings include “Sexuality and Syntax in Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse,” “Robinson Crusoe: Canibalism and Capitalism,” and “The Chaneysville Incident: The Belly of the Text.”

Situating Contact Functioning

The “contact functioning” is a critical concept in modern psychoanalytic theory and practice. The center of the concept focuses on an observable fact-the patient directly contacts the analyst. This direct contact provides a unique opportunity to discover, develop and coevolve (Bateson, 1979) 1 the relationship of analysand and analyst as well as the internal relationships of each.

In this essay I am interested in situating the contact functioning in historical and theoretic frames in which it has not usually been viewed in order to highlight and appreciate more of its facets. I would like to bring contact functioning out of its clinical moment so that when it is returned, the clinician might experience more thoughts and feelings about it. My primary focus in this situating enterprise is to place “interpretation” next to contact functioning. Specifically, I review various difficulties analysts have raised with the timing of interpretations. This will illuminate the central importance of following the contact functioning. To begin, we can look at the original formulations.

Spotnitz (1985) speaks of the contact functioning as “occasional verbal attempts to gratify an immediate need for words from the analyst” (p. 154), or as “direct attempts to elicit some personal information about the analyst or to involve the analyst in some emotional problem he (the patient) is unable to express in words” (1963, p. 54).

The volume by Grünbaum includes an introduction by Philip Holzman and ten essays by Grünbaum based on previously published materials and lectures. Over half of the monograph is a sequel to the author's 1984 book, The Foundations of Psychoanalysis. Some of the chapters respond to critics of his earlier work, Wallerstein, Edelson and Strenger. Other chapters critique hermeneutics and Popper's declarations on psychoanalysis as non-science. The volume in toto presents Grünbaum's ideas on the principal issues in establishing the validity of the clinical theory of psychoanalysis. He begins with the failure of clinical data to support Freud's cardinal causal hypotheses. He then questions the reliance of psychoanalysis on clinical data to claim validation of its theories.

Grünbaum agrees in principle with Edelson, Mackay and Strenger, each writing independently on the causal role of unconscious processes, when he writes that “hidden motives cry out for careful scrutiny” (p. 3).

These two volumes present Jean-Michel Petot's comprehensive and exhaustive inquiry into the origin, formation, and evolution of Melanie Klein's views on psychoanalytic theory and technique. This is an important task considering the complexity, ambiguity, and many inconsistencies in Melanie Klein's work. As Petot emphasizes throughout, Klein's theory is hardly a closed system. Klein's important theoretical constructs have gone through many revisions, but have not been always re-integrated into the general body of her theoretical system. As such the meaning of so many of her concepts such as introjection, internal object, imago, splitting, paranoid and depressive positions, etc., depends very much on the specific historical phase of the development of her ideas. It would be indeed difficult for the students of psychoanalysis to understand Klein's theory by reading a few of her isolated papers, particularly those of the early years. For those interested in understanding Melanie Klein's work, Petot provides an excellent theoretical base.

Petot's ability to bring clarity to some of the most esoteric thinking in psychoanalysis is most impressive. His work is certainly in the best tradition of French scholarship. There is no linguistic obfuscation and intellecutal mystification of simple ideas. Actually, Petot tries to demystify much of the esoteric, and at times confusing, language of the Kleinian theoretical writings. He also tries to maintain a relatively objective analytic stance for the evaluation of the scientific value of Melanie Klein's work. Here he is not always successful. In short, Petot has produced some very good work. Much credit should be due to Christine Trollope for an excellent translation of the language of such a complex and difficult area of inquiry.

This richly detailed and well researched volume weaves a tapestry filled with female characters connected to Freud either as family members, patients or followers. Written by Lisa Appignanesi, a British novelist, and John Forresters, her husband, a lecturer in the History and Philosophy of Science at Cambridge University and a noted Freud scholar, this book both entertains and instructs. Although often as engrossing as a novel, this book offers an intellectual history of the times as well as a serious study of Freud's theories about female sexuality and the contributions to his theories made by his female follwers.

In response to the controversy that has surrounded Freud's ideas about female psychosexual development since the Women's Rights movement of the 1960s, the authors frame this volume with an introduction entitled “Freud on Trial” and a concluding chapter entitled “Feminism and Psychoanalysis.” These discussions of psychopolitical debates are conscientious and informative but it is the lively descriptions of many intelligent and independent women that inform this work and bring it to life.

Amalie Nathansohn Freud was the first woman in Freud's life: the mother about whom he revealed so very little. Although she was consciously revered in teh traditional sense, she became unique when Freud cast her in the mold of a sexual being, as a key player in the oedipal triangle, the resolution of which he identified as the determining factor in psycho-sexual development.

Martha Bernays, “an adored sweetheart in youth, and a beloved wife in maturity” (p. 1) replaced Amalie in Freud's adult affections. He was as protective of his relationship with her as he was of that with his mother. We know more about their four-year engagement than we know about their fifty-three years of married life.

Classical analysts consider conflict and compromise to be the best organizing concepts in psychoanalysis. For them the drives (libidinal and aggressive) are the wellsprings of human motivation. Indulging drives in fact or fantasy may give rise to unpleasure and therefore to conflict. It is the frustration of drive-related needs and wishes that leads to psychic pain. Clinicans committed to conflict theory as the keystone of psychoanalysis will say, as Elizabeth Lord Mayer says, “talk about practically anything from a psychoanalytic point of view and you find you're talking about conflict.” While there is general agreement that conflict exists in all of us, disagreement arises when we seek to define conflict and describe its origins, that is, say exactly what is in conflict or decide what to do about it in the clinical situation.

This book contains six theoretical chapters, followed by four chapters which discuss the six theoretical chapters, and five rebutals. In one theoretical chapter, Jacob Arlow contrasts the concept of conflict with the parallel concepts of trauma and deficit. For Arlow the type of object relationships that give rise to deficits are inexorably involved in the process of conflict and therefore not excluded from its overall influence. Whereas for Arlow all conflict arises from the drives, other theorists believe that deficiencies in ego functions are unrelated to the sexual and aggressive conflicts. They believe that the roots of the problem lie in the failures of the mother's capacity to nurture or empathize with her infant. Such trauma causes basic defects in crucial internalization processes.

A second theoretical chapter by Dale Boesky describes and illustrates the organizing concept of compromise formation as conceived by Charles Brenner.

In his fascinating and idosyncratic book about psychotherapy, If You Meet the Buddha on the Road, Kill Him, Sheldon B. Kopp likens the journey of the client to Dante's journey through Hell. He says: “No patient in psychotherapy can recover his own beauty and innocence without first facing the ugliness and evil in himself…The ways in which we live, the experience of our own sinful souls, still is itself our only Hell.”

As clinicians, we sit each day with people who struggle to face their own private Hells, their forbidden desires, their secret shames. We sit with daughters who despise their mothers, and mothers who envy their daughters; fathers who abandon their sons, and sons who plot to murder their fathers. We meet liars, cheaters, rageaholics, drug addicts, and sexual misfits, many of whom look like the most upright citizens to the outside world.

This split between the official self and the disowned self, the Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde within us all, has been the subject of much discussion in various schools of psychology. Whether it's dubbed as the alter ego, the lower self, the double, or the shadow, it contains a Pandora's box of repressed feelings, thoughts, and behaviours that eventually surface during the course of therapy.

Introduction

Mr. L is a young adult male with HIV disease who can't decide if he wants to live or die. That is how he frames his problem. It is not an intellectual debate. He may, in fact, die soon. In his intial interview, he stated his dilemma bluntly:

If I don't get in touch with my emotions I will surely die. I might die anyway but my feelings will kill me if I don't understand them better.

This was a patient who had spent the past ten years drug-addicted and promiscuous. He felt that being HIV positive was just punishment for his lifestyle. He condemned himself just as his strict religious upbringing had condemned him. This is how he understood his experience.

His struggle jolted me right from the start because it frightened me. I was not at all certain that I wanted to treat a terminally ill man who might die while he was in treatment. My grandiosity that I would cure him frightened me even more. I knew intellectually that analysis might not effect remission in such a dramatic somatic symptom as AIDS, but I wanted to believe that it could, that it could arrest any deterioration.

Dr. Sternbach, in a most human and unpretentious delivery, presents us with more than fifty years of his development from a refugee struggling as a frightened, insecure, non-English speaking young therapist to a senior statesman in our profession. He presents the concept of supervision as “liberation” and focuses on liberating the tension in the relationship as a precondition to any successful work. An atmosphere of comfort for both parties is essential. I interpret (pardon the experession) some of Dr. Sternbach's early anxiety with his supervisor as a fear of exposure not only to feelings of inadequacy but also to what may have been an unrecognized need for comfort. He stresses the importance of enjoying one's work with fun and humor at times, the pleasure of shared responsibility, and the security of having a supervisor. We certainly can understand this. It is interesting to hear how Dr. Spotnitz and he learned through experience that premature interpretation led to the loss of their supervisees. Dr. Sternbach confirms our ideas that no matter what the theoretical or technical position, the supervisor and the analyst take a creative flexibility or departure from the parameters of treatment—as exemplified by his sojourn with the child to Woolworth's—which can and often does resolve a patient's resistance, He is mindful of the supervisor's primary goal, to resolve the analyst's resistance to successfully resolving the patient's resistance to progressive communication. The case of the “fucking” duel led ultimately to a good result, but it is geneally better to plan an intervention with an idea of its outcome, rather than to respond impulsively to an induced feeling.

In his own inimitable dialogue format, Dr. Marshall vividly traces and brings to life the development of supervisory concepts and practice.

I was impressed by the four participants who worked hard to create a group climate and to help each other develop a cohesive atmosphere in which the audience could participate as a functioning unit. The four participants, working under difficult circumstances, depicted how a modern grup analyst conducts group and how he or she should be helped to function by the group

To work as a modern group analyst requires flexibility. The analyst has to have the ability to tolerate the emotions without acting on them, all the while working at the job of resolving group resistances as they appear in the group. A special problem that faces a modern group analyst is the aggressive emotion engendered by the possibly psychotic individuals with whom the modern group analyst may work. If the group analyst cannot manage the aggressive feeling, his work will be impaired.

It is clear that the four group analysts want to create an atmosphere which would expose the audience and themselves to the kind of emotions a modern group analyst is subject to when treating possibly psychotic individuals, be it in a therapy, supervisory, or training group. The task was multiple. First they tried to create an atmosphee common to a group situaiton. Second they tried to help each other to communicate the emotional state they were in. Third they tried to describe the emotional state they were in. Third they tried to describe the emotional problems that could occur in a group setting. Fourth they tried to illustrate how these emotional problems could be resolved by the modern group analyst. To a certain extent they were successful because people in the audience were subjected to a multitude of feelings they didn't understand, and so fell into a psychological state difficult for them to respond to.

A patient should be comfortable throughout the analysis. The analyst should strive to make the experience one in which it is a pleasure to come and say everything.

Hyman Spotnitz

Introduction

Discomfort serves as a resistance when it interferes with progressive communication. The patient who can say “I am comfortable” is in the best possible position to freely express his thoughts, memories and feelings. In its simplest definition, discomfort describes a state of physical or mental uneasiness, while comfort can be described as a state of contented well-being. The analyst has the responsibility for facilitating a comfortable environment for himself and for his patient. The degree to which discomfort on the part of the patient and/or the analyst serves to hinder this accomplishment is highlighted in this paper. This is an issue that does not appear to have been addressed directly either by Freud or contemporary psychoanalysts.

Freud (1913) made reference to what he called ceremonial observance regarding the position in which the treatment is carried out. “I hold on to the plan of getting the patient to lie on a sofa while I sit behind him out of his sight” (p. 133). He then goes on to give his reasons, both historical and personal.

This paper seeks to integrate two seemingly disparate areas and themes in the fields of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis: (1) The tendency of the child to be a therapist of the parent, especially as delineated by Searles (1975); (2) Filial therapy, which is the use of a parent as therapist. Marshall (1983) had begun the synthesis of these two areas by describing a process termed “sequence therapy” which denotes the progressive resolution of individual, dyadic, and group resistances operating in a family system.

The Child as Therapeutic Agent

What would prompt a child to be a therapeutic agent for the parent? The most parsimonious answer may be that caring for the parent has survival value. Without the parent, the baby/child dies or becomes defective. Searles (1975) hypothesized “… that innate among man's most powerful striving toward his fellow men, beginning in the earliest years and even earliest months of life, is an essentially psychotherapeutic striving” (p. 95). Earlier, Searles (1959) had introduced the idea that the child may remain in a symbiotic relationship with the mother in order for the mother to be sane. Marshall (1983) cites a case of an adolescent girl, eager to leave home, who formulated a plan to give birth to a baby and deed it to her symbiotic mother in order to prevent her mother's depression.

When I prepared this paper on supervision, I wondered whether I should use the Peter Gay-Ernest Jones dialogue (Marshall, 1991) because the degree of playfulness and unorthodoxy that I might portray probably would not be consonant with their positions and statures. Since I hold Peter Gay in the highest esteem and consider him to be the outstanding contemporary Freud scholar, I could not in all good conscience use his name in the following fashion. I consider Ernest Jones one of the prominent leaders in the psychoanalytic field, a man who had devoted his entire life to advancing the art and science of psychoanalysis. Since his position in the psychoanalytic world cannot be compromised nor misunderstood, I am taking this opportunity to use Ernest Jone's name to help enliven and clarify a subject which is ordinarily heavy and complex. Therefore, let us imagine that Ernest Jones is paying a visit not to Peter Gay, but to this author.

Marshall: Welcome to my earthly abode, Ernest. What brings about this great honor?

Jones: I did want to return Peter Gay's visit and to see what the colonies are up to these days in terms of tea and supervision. I understand that you have made impressive gains in the area of supervision.

Marshall: Yes, as I look ovr the past 40 years I discern some significant shifts.

Introduction

The growing awareness of the effectiveness of psychotherapy with all segments of the population is well understood and acknowledged. In the field of geriatric medicine, psychotherapy has become an integral aspect of the multidisciplinary approach to treating the elderly. Many nursing homes contract with agencies for a consultant to provide psychotherapy to their residents and patients.

Elderly persons residing in nursing homes encounter major changes in their lives when giving up independent living situations and making the transition to institutional living/life. For this age group, losses fall into these categories: physical, mental, relationships, material possessions, finacnes and independence. Individuals react to losses in varied ways, such as dpression, anxiety, confusion, helplessness, verbal abusiveness and physically disruptive behaviors.

As a consultant, I assessed and provided psychotherapy to individuals in two nursing homes. In one of the nursing homes, the psychiatrist presented the unusual case of an isolated, verabally disruptive patient and requested my opinion. This paper describes the treatment and outcome of basically silent mirroring of the patient's bodily movements, with a minimum of verbalization, over a three-mongth period.

David Rosenthal PHD C.S.W.

David Rosenthal

171 East 89th Street

David Rosenthal   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is a graduate of the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis and currently on the faculty at NYU School of Social Work, PCNJ, RCMP and Adelphi University Post-Masters Program in Clinical Social Work.

The prognostic intervention is one of many modern analytic techniques designed to help patients verbalize their thoughts, feelings, and impulses constructively in group therapy. It is used when group members are acting upon their feelings instead of expressing them in words, and when the overall functioning of the group is jeopardized. The term “prognostic” refers to the therapist's efforts to head off the potential impact of treatment-destructive resistances before their damaging effects are realized. The prognostic intervention is a unique way for the therapist to confront group-destructive behaviors, and to initiate a “pre-emptive strike” against these damaging forces.

The technique is derived from the pioneering work of Hyman Spotnitz, and from the body of joining techniques he developed. It has been used in group therapy workshops and seminars designed to provide experiences in emotional learning. Thus, the technique has been taught in an experiential manner and, in this way, has been handed down to generations of modern analysts. This teaching approach has been discussed with great clarity by Phyllis Meadow in her paper on modern analytic training (1988).

The prognostic intervention was developed and refined by Leslie Rosenthal, who established its use as a tool for resolving treatment-destructive resistances in group therapy. The technique has been illustrated in a number of his papers discussing resistance in groups (1971, 1976, 1979, 1985).

Dr. Bernstein: (To audience) The three people sitting on the platform with me, plus Dr. Hyman Spotnitz (who though invisible is also with us in spirit), considering all of the groups they have led and all of the years they have practiced, have each probably treated more people in group analysis their lifetimes then almost anyone else in our profession.

It was to avoid countertransference resistance that Freud (1912) recommended that would should model ourselves on the surgeon and put aside all our feelings, and concentrate our mental forces on the single aim of performing the operation as skillfully as possible (p. 115).

In psychoanalysis, every major obstacle has paved the way for new discoveries. When Freud first realized that patients were more influenced by their feelings about him than they were their desire to profit from treatment, he discovered a major obstacle to treatment. However he found a way to make use of this nuisance-as transference (or resistance to transference, or transferennce reistance), it became the new cornerstone of treatment. Similarly, in doing supervision we often find that the analyst's countertransference (or resistance to countertransference or countertransference resistance) leads directly to the problem and to its solution.

The Current Scene

It was and is sometimes suprising to find that modern analysis is still in the vanguard. Iatrogenic Blocks to Therapeutic Progress: A Study of Countertransference Resistances

Stanford Bazilian MD

Stanford Bazilian

313 South 16th St.
Philadelphia, PA 19102

Stanford Bazilian   Certified psychiatrist and psychoanalyst in private practice on Philadelphia. He is a training and supervising analyst and Director of Admissions at the Philadelphia School of Psychoanalysis. His previous writings include “latrogenic Emotional Problems Associated with Ward Rounds” and “An Experimental Method of Evolving a Theory of Therapeutic Technique.”

Introduction

In many psychoanalytic cases adverse neurotic patterns manifested by patients appear to be reactions to attitudes and/or interventions by the analyst. These reactions may be attributed to particular treatment processes and techniques.

Currently, no precise terminology in the literature specifically describes this phenomenon. The closest references to it is the more general term iatrogenic (Hinsie & Campbell, 1970, p. 371), which identifies any treatment technique that causes adverse reactions in the patient but without direct reference to the psychotherapist. It would appear, however, that in the psychotherapeutic relationship this condition warrants a more precise term, not only because the frequency and scope of occurrence are extensive, but because it would prove beneficial to study and understand this phenomenon. To delineate its origins, causes, characteristics, and outcomes would lead to understanding it and learning how to use it for the benefit of the patient. In my experience I have encountered many manifestations of this situation, as have a number of colleagues with whom I have consulted regarding this problem. Since there is no term available to explain these reactions, it might be of practical use to adopt one.

The Supervisor as the Liberator**

Oscar Sternbach J.D.

Oscar Sternbach

12 West 96th Street
15C New York, Ny 10035

Oscar Sternbach   Started his psychoanalytic studies in Vienna and came to this country in 1939. He has been a psychoanalyst in private practice for many years. He has also been on the faculties of several psychoanalytic institutes, among them the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is the author of many articles about the history, theory and technique of adult and child psychoanalysis.

Liberating supervision, or supervision as liberation, are the names which have come to my mind as titles for this paper. Supervision—the name alone can induce tension, anxiety, or at least apprehension in the growing psychoanalyst. Of course it does not have to have this effect. The supervisory relationship will always depend on the two personalities involved. But in many people the inequality of the situation alone is apt to arouse the whole oedipal constellatin of conflicted feelings. What will be examined and discussed is nothing less than one's entire spectrum of knowledge, one's skill in social intercourse, and one's anxieties, which one would like to keep private until they are overcome. In this situation, where one can be looked through and through, vulnerabilties are naked and raw.

Those sessions with the patient, being unsure of what the right word was or which one should be used, are difficult enough. There might have been anger expressed, or just a visible distrust, a resistance to the process of analysis. One expects it, of course, but when confronted, the experience can be devastating. And always the thought, will the patient come back? what if he were to stop coming? I do not have to say more to illustrate the average supervisory situation, particularly of the beginner.

The supervisor can also be a beginner.

*This paper was originally presented at the CMPS Conference: Transference and Resistance in the Supervisory Process, November 7, 1992.37

Benito Perri PHD

Benito Perri

31 West 12th Street
New York, NY 10011

Benito Perri   Founder and Executive Director of the Long Island Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is a faculty member and training analyst at a number of psychoanalytic institutes. He is the author of “Modern Analysis and the Negative Therapeutic Reaction.” Dr. Perri is in private practice in New York City and Cold Spring Harbor.

“The situation between the supervisor and the student is analogous to that between the supervisee and the patient.” So writes Spotnitz (1976, p. 217). Emotions aroused in the supervisor are key to understanding the dilemmas supervisees face with their patients. Narcisistic patients induce primitive feelings in their analyst and attempt to recreate past object relationships in the transference. The same process occurs in supervision. This paper will highlight strategies for dealing with this process, identified as projective identification.

A few years ago, one female supervisee, an unusually bright and gifted clinician with a flourishing practice, was going through a particularly difficult period with a number of female patients, each of whom was constantly criticizing her and complaining bitterly that not only was she not making progress, but her life had gotten worse. My supervisee was being made to feel inadequate and flawed, which only served to enrage her. She became paralyzed in her thinking and ability to function, out of fear that she would lose control and kill her patients. At the same time she felt an urgent pressure to do something to relieve the pain and suffering of her patients.

In supervisory sessions, as I attempted to help her analyze her patients rather than “do something” for them, I was told, “Don't explore with me; just tell me what to do. “My efforts to explore were met with pain, anguish, and anger. If I suggested an intervention, she claimed it would only meet with more rage from her patients—rage that had become intolerable.

*This paper was originally presented at the CMPS Conference: Transference and Resistance in the Supervisory Process, November 7, 1992.59

Being A Character: Psychoanalysis and Self Experience. Christopher Bollas. New York: Hill and Wang, 1992. 294 pp.

Barbara Steif

Barbara Steif

Barbara Steif  

What does it mean to be a character? If, as Christopher Bollas writes, “Wisdom is measured by increased uncertainty about the meanings of our self, or of life” (p. 61), then these thoughtful essays urge us to deepen our wisdom about the human conditions and the endeavor of psychoanalysis. Bollas leads the analytic debate into the realm of reverie, and he succeds brilliantly in extracting from our elusive subjectivity a compassionate grasp of how we may, or may not, connect with one another.

It is Bollas' belief that each of us possesses a unique idiom of psychic organization which constitutes the core of our self. As we grow, he says, this inner presence becomes more complex, and more mysterious to our consciousness. Indeed, the true self is unconsciousness, profoundly known yet unthought, and its joy comes from the surrender to experience that transforms subjectivity into reality. To be a character, then, is to find the unconscious idiom of one's self released into being. Bollas suggests that this articulation of the simple experiencing self is the dream work of life. It is accomplished through the selection and use of objects, both animate and not, that transform our “latent deep structure into surface expression” (p. 54).

Bollas proposes a “collisional dialectic” (p. 60) to describe the process by which our selves are nourished by the object world. With each encounter, our subjectivity is newly informed, and we gain a history of highly condensed psychic textures
